title: Diwali

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pushpaka's flight home. Rama pointed out the places below to Sita, one by one, the whole journey in reverse. Did you look back over a road you've traveled? Today the chariot comes down, and someone has been waiting fourteen years. Day six hundred sixty-two.

Ask almost anyone who grew up with Diwali why the lamps are lit, and you'll often hear the same answer: because Rama came home. The whole city lit lamps so he could find his way. It's a lovely picture. So here's something surprising. Open Valmiki's Ramayana to the homecoming, and look for the lamps. Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music, roads sprinkled with water, a crowd so big it fills the streets. A city lit by rows of lamps isn't the picture he paints. The lamps seem to have arrived later, as the story moved into the festival. Today we read what Valmiki does tell: the homecoming itself, and the man at the center of it, who isn't Rama.
screen: `WHY THE LAMPS?` → `BECAUSE RAMA CAME HOME.` → `WHAT VALMIKI ACTUALLY SAYS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday ended with Hanuman sent ahead to watch Bharata's face. Remember Bharata: he never wanted the throne. For fourteen years he has lived outside Ayodhya, in a village called Nandigram, in bark clothing, with matted hair, ruling only as a caretaker, with Rama's sandals set on the throne. His face gave its answer before he said a word. Now Valmiki turns to what Bharata does with the news, and Bharata's joy is the center of the chapter. He orders the roads leveled and watered, the city decorated, the musicians out. Then the pushpaka comes into sight, and Bharata goes out to meet it on foot, carrying the sandals. When Rama steps down, Bharata bows, and then he does the thing he's been waiting fourteen years to do. He puts the sandals back on his brother's feet. The kingdom, he says, was a deposit left with me; I'm giving it back. That's Valmiki's homecoming. Not lamps, exactly, but a promise kept on both sides. Rama kept his word to his father; Bharata kept his to Rama. Over the centuries, the night Rama came home became one of the stories Diwali tells, especially across North India. Other regions tell other stories for the same night, and we'll meet those in the festival days ahead.
screen: `BHARATA HEARS THE NEWS.` · `ROADS WATERED, CITY DRESSED.` · `THE SANDALS GO BACK ON.` · `A DEPOSIT, RETURNED.` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes close or rest low. Bring to mind something you're holding for someone else: a key, a secret, a job, a child for an afternoon, a promise. Picture handing it back, whole, the way Bharata handed back the sandals. Notice how that feels in your chest and shoulders. Then let the picture go and rest with the breath until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. In Valmiki, the homecoming is Bharata's day: roads watered, a city dressed, and the sandals placed back on Rama's feet.
Your line: Diwali. Today, give back one thing you've been holding for someone, a borrowed book, a message, a favor owed, and give it back whole. Day six hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Ramayana reciters often read the homecoming and the meeting with Bharata as their own episode, and in much of North India families tell Rama's return as the reason Diwali lamps are lit.

myth: Valmiki describes the city lighting rows of lamps for Rama
Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music and watered roads. the lamps came later, with the festival.
Bharata waits on the throne for Rama to come to him
he goes out on foot to meet the chariot, carrying the sandals.

a deposit, he says, and now he gives it back.

fork.setup: you're Bharata. after fourteen years, Rama's chariot comes down. what do you do first?
options: wait on the throne for him.
walk out to meet him, carrying his sandals.
send the army to escort him.
fork.reveal: he goes out on foot with the sandals, bows, and puts them back on his brother's feet.

original.note: Sanskrit pādukā: a sandal. Rama's sandals sat on the throne for fourteen years.

trapdoor: what you thought: Diwali's lamps come straight from Valmiki's homecoming.
what it means: Valmiki's homecoming is flags, flowers, music, and Bharata returning the kingdom; the lamps came with the festival.
what a scholar hears: in the Yuddha Kanda, Rama sends Hanuman ahead partly to test Bharata's heart, and Bharata calls the kingdom a deposit he now returns.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 125–127 (Hanuman sent to Bharata; Bharata's preparations; the meeting)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; the critical edition differs. Confirm.

Rama's instruction to Hanuman to watch Bharata's face, and 'let him keep it', are paraphrased; confirm the sense.
